summary:
Lunar Atlas is a browser-based decision aid that helps mission planners compare 16 lunar landing sites (Apollo 11–17, seven Artemis III candidate regions, VIPER’s Nobile Rim 1, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang’e 4) on sunlight, terrain, temperature, water-ice indications and Earth line of sight. For each site we precomputed hourly Sun and Earth geometry over 60 days, with a 360-degree terrain horizon that accounts for lunar curvature.

The problem: near the poles the Sun skims the horizon, so a few hundred metres of terrain can decide between near-constant power and long darkness, and Earth can vanish behind a ridge.

Our solution brings it together in one app: a 360-degree panorama, a 3D Moon textured with NASA LROC and LOLA data, a polar sky plot, a weighted six-factor scorecard, and a Plan tab where users enter their own mission constraints. Every layer carries clear provenance labels, and coarse hydrogen data carries footprint warnings.
details:
What exactly does it do?
Lunar Atlas lets a user choose any of 16 lunar sites (Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17, seven Artemis III candidate regions, VIPER’s Nobile Rim 1, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang’e 4) and see, hour by hour, when the Sun and Earth are visible or hidden behind local terrain. Sites can then be compared side by side. The app has five areas. Dashboard gives a ranked overview. Explore has a 360-degree horizon panorama with a time scrubber, a 3D Moon, a cinematic Moon Story view and a polar sky plot. Compare has a multi-site matrix and a six-factor weighted scorecard (terrain safety, illumination, thermal environment, water-ice potential, communications, data confidence) with CSV and PNG export. Plan lets users enter their own mission constraints, and pass/fail results and a schedule-slip heatmap appear only after they do. Data shows provenance, limitations and a Provenance Inspector for every layer.

How does it work?
There are two tiers. An offline Python pipeline computes, for each site, a 1,441-point hourly time series covering 1 January to 2 March 2027. It includes Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation, libration, angular diameters, and the visible fraction of each disc. It also builds a 360-ray terrain horizon with lunar curvature drop (d squared over 2R, R = 1,737.4 km) and a 2 m observer height, plus terrain, thermal and hydrogen indicators and a six-factor score, all saved as static JSON. A React and TypeScript web app then loads that data and renders everything in the browser with no backend, so it works offline and deploys as a static site. Geometric Earth line of sight is kept separate from a verified radio link; the +2 degree clearance is labelled “assumed”.

What benefits does it offer?
It gives planners, students and the public a free, transparent way to compare sites on lighting and communications in one place. It shows why polar lighting is controlled by terrain at the scale of a few hundred meters. Every layer is labelled with its source, and uncertainty is stated openly, for example a footprint warning on coarse hydrogen data and no invented vehicle limits.

What do you hope to achieve?
We want a first-pass site comparison tool that shortens early mission analysis and teaches how lunar lighting and Earth visibility work. Next, we plan to ingest the full LOLA polar elevation models, SPICE kernels and JPL Horizons directly, so every number traces back to a NASA product. We also plan to add relay-orbiter modelling for far-side and shadowed sites.

Tools, languages, hardware and software used
Front end: TypeScript, React 18, Vite 6, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, d3, three.js, Vitest and lucide-react. Pipeline: Python 3.12 and NumPy, with optional SpiceyPy and rasterio hooks. Deployment is a static build on Netlify. No special hardware was used. AI coding assistants helped generate and refactor code, tests and documentation.

Current status and limitations
This release uses an analytical lunar ephemeris model rather than live SPICE or Horizons queries. Terrain horizons, local relief, and the thermal and hydrogen values are publication-derived models based on published LOLA, Diviner and LEND results, not extracted from raw rasters. The NASA data used directly is the LROC and LOLA textures for the 3D Moon plus published site coordinates. Ingestion code for the real products is included. Lunar Atlas is a decision aid and educational tool, not certified for flight operations.
